items.q: Which statement is best supported by the data in the table?
options: The two hydrogen-bonding liquids have the two highest heats of vaporization.
Heat of vaporization rises steadily as boiling point rises across the four liquids.
Polar liquids have a higher specific heat than nonpolar liquids in this table.
Surface tension rises as specific heat falls across the four liquids.

items.q: Neither acetone nor hexane forms hydrogen bonds, and acetone is polar while hexane is not. Yet hexane has the higher boiling point and the higher specific heat. What is the most reasonable conclusion from these two liquids?
options: Other, weaker attractions also matter, so hydrogen bonding explains the large differences but not every small one.
Hexane molecules probably form a few hydrogen bonds with each other that the table does not report.
Nonpolar molecules attract one another more strongly than polar molecules do, in general.
The hexane values are likely measurement errors, since a nonpolar liquid would be expected to rank last on each of these properties.

items.q: A runner loses 900 g of sweat in an hour, and all of it evaporates from her skin. Using the table's heat of vaporization for water, how much heat, in kilojoules, does this evaporation remove from her body? Round to the nearest whole kilojoule.

An engineer considers replacing water with methanol in a cooling system that removes heat by evaporating the liquid. To remove the same amount of heat, how would the mass of liquid that must evaporate change?
options: About half as much methanol would need to evaporate, since it evaporates more easily.
About the same mass, since both liquids form hydrogen bonds.
About twice as much methanol would need to evaporate.
About four times as much, since methanol's surface tension is about a third of water's.

items.q: Water and methanol both form hydrogen bonds between molecules, yet water's surface tension is more than three times methanol's. Which explanation is most consistent with the table?
options: Each methanol molecule is nonpolar except for a small charged region, so it attracts its neighbors weakly.
Water molecules are larger and heavier than methanol molecules, so each one pulls on its neighbors at the surface harder.
Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds, a denser network than methanol's single O–H group allows.
Methanol molecules form covalent bonds with each other that pull the surface molecules inward less strongly.

items.q: Which description of the graph is accurate?
options: Acetone produced the largest, fastest drop, but its thermometer was also the first to warm back up.
Water produced the largest drop in temperature, because it has the highest heat of vaporization of the three.
The three liquids cooled their thermometers by about the same amount, but at different speeds.
Methanol cooled its thermometer for longer than water did.

items.q: Acetone has the lowest heat of vaporization of the three liquids, yet it produced the largest temperature drop. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Acetone has a lower specific heat than water, so the cloth soaked in acetone held less heat to begin with and cooled sooner.
With no hydrogen bonds to break, acetone evaporated so fast that it removed more heat per minute, though less per gram.
Acetone molecules absorb heat as they form hydrogen bonds with the cotton of the cloth.
Acetone removed more total heat than water did over the 8 minutes.

items.q: Use the heats of vaporization from the table of four liquids (methanol 1,100 J/g; acetone 500 J/g). By the time each cloth was dry, how many more joules had evaporation of the methanol removed than evaporation of the acetone? Round to the nearest whole joule.
Why did the student include a thermometer wrapped in a dry cloth?
options: To show that a dry cotton cloth absorbs heat from the thermometer bulb as the fan blows room air across it.
To measure how fast water vapor from the other cloths spread through the room.
To provide a fourth liquid for comparison with water, methanol and acetone.
To show the effect of the fan and cloth alone, so extra cooling of the wet thermometers can be credited to evaporation.

items.q: The experiment is repeated with the same 22 °C air but at 90% humidity, so water evaporates much more slowly. Predict how each value for the water-soaked thermometer would change compared with the original run.

variables.name: Lowest temperature the water thermometer reaches
Time until the water cloth is dry
Heat removed per gram of water that does evaporate

items.q: By what factor did the hydrogen ion concentration in Beaker A (pure water) increase when the first 1 mL of acid was added? Give a whole number.
Which explanation best accounts for the difference between the beakers over the first 5 mL of acid?
options: Bicarbonate ions in Beaker B combined with most added hydrogen ions to form carbonic acid, so few stayed free.
Beaker B received fewer hydrogen ions per milliliter than Beaker A, because its solution was already partly acidic at the start.
Beaker B's carbonic acid released hydroxide ions that neutralized the added acid.
Water molecules in Beaker B formed hydrogen bonds with the added hydrogen ions and held them in place.

items.q: Between 15 mL and 25 mL of acid, the pH of Beaker B fell from 5.76 to 2.40. Which explanation is best supported by the data?
options: The bicarbonate ran out near 20 mL, so added hydrogen ions stayed free and the pH fell about as steeply as plain water's.
The carbonic acid that had formed began to release extra bicarbonate ions, which lowered the pH.
The later milliliters of acid were more concentrated than the earlier ones.
Beaker B was diluted by the 25 mL of added acid, so its bicarbonate and carbonic acid were too spread out to work together.

items.q: A student claims, "Beaker B keeps its pH near 7 no matter how much acid is added." Which evidence from the table most directly refutes this claim?
options: Beaker A's pH fell from 7.00 to 3.00 after just 1 mL of the acid was added.
Beaker B's pH fell from 7.00 to 6.89 after 1 mL of acid.
Beaker B's pH fell from 5.76 to 2.40 between 15 mL and 25 mL of acid.
Beaker B started at exactly the same pH as Beaker A.

items.q: A crystal of table salt (NaCl) dissolves in water. Which description of the water molecules closest to the ions is correct?
options: Oxygen atoms face the sodium ions, and hydrogen atoms face the chloride ions.
Hydrogen atoms face the sodium ions, and oxygen atoms face the chloride ions.
Water molecules form covalent bonds with the ions, sharing electrons with them.
Water molecules point in random directions, because the ions carry full charges rather than partial ones.

items.q: Suppose ice were denser than liquid water. What would most likely happen to a deep lake during a long, cold winter?
options: The lake would stay liquid longer, because sinking ice would carry cold away from the surface and leave warmer water on top.
Nothing would change, because the surface of a lake is the part that reaches 0 °C.
Ice would sink as it formed, so the lake could freeze from the bottom up, leaving little liquid water for fish.
The lake would freeze more slowly, because denser ice would hold more heat.

items.q: On a hot, dry afternoon a plant closes most of its stomata. Predict how each value changes over the next hour compared with when the stomata were open.

variables.name: Rate at which water moves up the xylem
Strength of each hydrogen bond between water molecules in the xylem

items.q: Which of these substances would you expect to dissolve readily in water? Select all that apply.
options: Table salt (NaCl), an ionic compound
Vegetable oil, made mostly of carbon and hydrogen
Candle wax, made of carbon and hydrogen
Methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, with one O–H group
Hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>, made of C–H and C–C bonds

items.q: In which bond are the shared electrons pulled most strongly toward one atom?
options: C–H, as in candle wax
O–H, in a water molecule
C–C, as in candle wax
H–H, in a hydrogen gas molecule

items.q: A student draws a hydrogen bond as a dashed line between a hydrogen atom of one water molecule and a hydrogen atom of a neighboring water molecule. What is wrong with the drawing?
options: Nothing; any two hydrogen atoms on neighboring molecules can form a hydrogen bond.
The line should be solid, because hydrogen bonds are as strong as covalent bonds.
Both hydrogens carry a partial positive charge and repel; a hydrogen bond links a δ+ hydrogen to a δ− oxygen.
Hydrogen bonds form inside one water molecule, so the dashed line should join each hydrogen to its own oxygen atom.

items.q: Which conclusion about sulfur is best supported by the data?
options: The algae used sulfur mainly to build proteins.
The algae used sulfur mainly to build nucleic acids and ATP.
The algae spread sulfur about evenly among the five fractions of the cell.
The algae used sulfur mainly to build carbohydrates, as they did with carbon.

items.q: About 22% of the phosphorus-32 was found in the lipid fraction. Which claim does this evidence best support?
options: Some of the algae's lipids contain phosphorus, most likely as phosphate groups.
The algae converted phosphorus atoms into carbon atoms to build the lipids they needed.
Lipids are the main place where algae store phosphorus for later use in their nucleic acids.
Most lipids in the algae contain phosphorus, since 22% is a large share of the label.

items.q: A fifth culture gets light, carbon dioxide, phosphate and sulfate but no nitrogen source. Over the next day, which outcome is most likely?
options: The algae keep making new proteins but stop making new nucleic acids.
The algae can still make sugars and many lipids, but making new proteins and nucleic acids slows.
The algae stop photosynthesis, since each molecule in the cell contains nitrogen.
The algae use the extra phosphorus in place of the missing nitrogen when they build new amino acids and nucleic acids.

items.q: The nitrogen-15 culture took up 2.40 mmol of labeled nitrogen. How many millimoles of it ended up in nucleic acids? Give your answer to two decimal places.
Why can the researchers treat the labeled atoms as a fair guide to where ordinary nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and carbon go in the algae?
options: Labeled atoms are taken up faster than ordinary atoms, so they reach more of the cell's molecules in a day.
Isotopes have the same protons and electrons as ordinary atoms, so cells use them in the same chemistry.
Isotopes have extra electrons, which makes them easy to detect without changing where they go.
Radioactive atoms damage the molecules they enter, which makes those molecules easier to separate into fractions.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the data for Chamber 1 (the plant)?
options: Carbon dioxide fell while the lamp was on and rose more slowly after it was switched off.
Carbon dioxide fell at a steady rate for the whole 120 minutes.
Carbon dioxide rose while the lamp was on and fell after it was switched off.
Carbon dioxide rose after the lamp went off, at about the same speed it had fallen.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the rise in carbon dioxide in Chamber 1 after the lamp was switched off?
options: Plants switch from photosynthesis to cellular respiration at night, so the plant began releasing carbon dioxide.
Respiration continued in the plant's cells, and without light, photosynthesis stopped taking carbon dioxide up.
Carbon dioxide stored in the soil leaked into the chamber once the lamp stopped warming the soil.
Without light, the plant broke down the oxygen it had made earlier into carbon dioxide.

items.q: On average, by how many ppm per minute did the carbon dioxide in Chamber 1 fall while the lamp was on (0 to 60 minutes)? Give your answer to two decimal places.

Suppose the plant's cellular respiration ran at the same rate in the light as it did in the dark (60 to 120 minutes). Which value best estimates how fast photosynthesis alone removed carbon dioxide while the lamp was on?
options: About 0.60 ppm per minute
About 1.65 ppm per minute
About 2.25 ppm per minute
About 2.85 ppm per minute

items.q: The plant and the 20 crickets are sealed together in one chamber under the lamp. Assuming each behaves as it did alone, what happens to carbon dioxide in the chamber air?
options: It rises, because the crickets release carbon dioxide faster than the plant can take it up.
It stays at 420 ppm, because the crickets' output and the plant's uptake cancel out.
It falls, but more slowly than with the plant alone, as the plant takes up carbon atoms the crickets release.
It falls faster than with the plant alone, because the crickets' breathing speeds up photosynthesis.

items.q: Which molecule carries a sulfhydryl group?
options: Molecule A
Molecule C
Molecule D
Molecule E

items.q: Molecule C does not dissolve in water. Which feature of its structure best explains this?
options: Its carboxyl group releases hydrogen ions, which makes it repel water molecules.
Most of the molecule is a chain of carbons carrying hydrogens, and C–H bonds are nonpolar.
It contains oxygen, which is highly electronegative and pulls electrons away from water.
It is much larger than a water molecule, and large molecules are too big to dissolve in water.

items.q: Which of the molecules are amino acids? Select all that apply.
options: Molecule A
Molecule B
Molecule C
Molecule D
Molecule E

items.q: Molecule F also has the formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, but its C=O group is in the middle of the carbon chain instead of at the end. How are Molecules B and F related?
options: They are isotopes, because they contain the same elements in the same amounts.
They are the same molecule, because a formula fully describes a molecule.
They are isomers: the same formula with different structures, so they can have different properties.
They differ on paper alone; moving a group along the chain does not change a molecule's behavior.

items.q: Which element is part of both proteins and nucleic acids but is absent from typical sugars and fats?
options: Oxygen
Carbon
Nitrogen
Sulfur

items.q: A farmer's soil test shows plenty of nitrogen but very little phosphorus. Which molecules will the crop have the most trouble building?
options: Nucleic acids and ATP, which contain phosphate groups.
Proteins, because each amino acid contains phosphorus.
Sugars, because phosphorus is part of each carbon skeleton.
Water, because plants build water from phosphorus taken in by their roots.

items.q: A carbon atom is part of a sugar molecule in one of your muscle cells. Trace it back through what you ate. Where was it most likely before it entered any living thing?
options: It did not exist yet; your body made it from the energy in the food you ate.
It was in carbon dioxide in the air, before a plant took it up by photosynthesis.
It was a nitrogen atom in the soil that a plant converted into carbon.
It has been in your body since birth, since atoms in the body are kept and reused for life.

items.q: A chemist adds a carboxyl group (–COOH) to the end of a hydrocarbon chain. In water, how is that end of the molecule most likely to behave?
options: It releases a hydrogen ion and becomes negatively charged.
It picks up a hydrogen ion and becomes positively charged.
It stays uncharged and nonpolar, like the rest of the chain.
It forms a bond with a second carboxyl group to link two chains together.

items.q: Which property of carbon best explains why it forms the skeletons of biological molecules?
options: Carbon is the most common element in the Earth's crust, so it is the easiest for cells to obtain.
Carbon is highly electronegative, so its bonds to hydrogen are strongly polar and dissolve in water.
Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds, so carbons can link into chains, branches and rings.
Carbon forms ionic bonds with oxygen, which hold large molecules together in water.

items.q: Which statement best describes the release of sugar monomers in Tube 1?
options: Monomers were released fastest at the start, and release slowed as time went on.
Monomers were released at a steady speed from the start to the end of the hour.
Monomers were released slowly at first and then faster and faster as the hour went on.
Release stopped at 40 minutes because the bonds in the polymer had been broken by then.

items.q: On average, how many mmol/L of sugar monomers were released per minute in Tube 1 during the first 10 minutes? Give your answer to two decimal places.
Which explanation best accounts for the slowing release of monomers in Tube 1 after about 20 minutes?
options: Fewer unbroken bonds between monomers were left, so there were fewer places where hydrolysis could happen.
The water in the tube was being used up by hydrolysis, so there was too little water left for more reactions.
The freed monomers began joining back together by dehydration synthesis at the same speed they were released.
The enzyme was turned into sugar monomers as it worked, so less enzyme remained over time.

items.q: What does Tube 3 allow the student to rule out?
options: That the polymer breaks down by itself in water at 37 °C without help.
That the monomers in Tube 1 came from the enzyme solution itself, not from the polymer.
That temperature affected how fast the enzyme broke down the polymer during the hour.
That this enzyme can also break down proteins in the same tube.

items.q: Predict how each quantity in Tube 1 changes between 0 and 60 minutes.

variables.name: Number of covalent bonds linking sugar monomers together
Number of water molecules in the tube
Total number of carbon atoms in the tube

items.q: How many water molecules are released when 25 monomers are joined into one straight, unbranched chain?
What is the mass, in daltons, of that straight chain of 25 monomers?
Some cells make a ring of 8 sugar monomers, in which the last monomer is also linked to the first. How many water molecules are released in making the ring from 8 free monomers?
A branched polymer of 40 sugar monomers has three side branches, and every monomer is part of one molecule with no rings. How many links between monomers does it have?
Two C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> monomers are joined by dehydration synthesis. What is the formula of the two-monomer product?
options: C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>24</sub>O<sub>12</sub>
C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>

items.q: Which group of biological macromolecules is usually not classed as a polymer?
options: Carbohydrates
Proteins
Nucleic acids
Lipids

items.q: When two monomers are joined by dehydration synthesis, where do the atoms of the released water molecule come from?
options: Both hydrogens and the oxygen come from one monomer, which loses a small piece of itself.
An –OH group from one monomer and an –H atom from the other monomer.
From the surrounding water, which is split so that the monomers can attach to each other.
From an enzyme, which donates an –OH and an –H each time it joins two monomers together.

items.q: A medicine blocks the gut enzyme that hydrolyzes a sugar polymer in food. A person takes it with a meal containing that polymer. Which result is most likely?
options: More of the polymer stays intact, so fewer sugar monomers are absorbed into the blood after the meal.
The polymer is absorbed into the blood whole, raising the sugar level in the blood faster than usual.
The polymer is broken down by dehydration synthesis instead, giving the same amount of monomers.
The body makes more water, which breaks the polymer down without the enzyme.

items.q: Put these events in order, from a protein in food to a new protein in a muscle cell.
options: Hydrolysis cuts the food protein into separate amino acids in the gut.
The amino acids are absorbed into the blood.
Muscle cells take up amino acids from the blood.
Dehydration synthesis joins the amino acids into a new protein chain, releasing water.

items.q: Two polymers are each made only of the same six-carbon sugar monomer. One dissolves easily and is quickly broken down by animals; the other forms tough fibers that most animals cannot break down. Which explanation is best?
options: One polymer contains a second kind of monomer that the other lacks, which changes its properties.
The monomers are linked in different ways, so the two chains have different shapes and properties.
The fibrous polymer has many more monomers, and long chains of a polymer are hard to break.
The fibrous polymer formed by hydrolysis and the soluble one formed by dehydration synthesis.

items.q: A two-monomer molecule is broken in half by hydrolysis. Which are the reactants of this reaction?
options: The two separate monomers.
The two-monomer molecule and a water molecule.
The two-monomer molecule by itself.
The two monomers and a water molecule.

items.q: Which of these are polymers? Select all that apply.
options: A protein chain of 300 amino acids
One six-carbon sugar molecule
A fat molecule from butter
A chain of 1,000 sugar units from a potato
A molecule of ATP

items.q: A 10.0 g sample of a long sugar polymer is completely hydrolyzed in water, and the monomers are dried and weighed. How does their total mass compare with 10.0 g?
options: Less than 10.0 g, because water is released as each bond in the polymer breaks.
Exactly 10.0 g, because hydrolysis rearranges the atoms of the polymer without adding any.
More than 10.0 g, because the atoms of one water molecule join the monomers at each bond broken.
It depends on how fast the enzyme worked, since a faster hydrolysis loses less mass.

items.q: Which polysaccharides did Enzyme B break down substantially? Select all that apply.
options: Starch
Glycogen
Cellulose
Chitin

items.q: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet Enzyme A broke down starch and not cellulose. Which explanation is best?
options: Cellulose is made of a different monosaccharide that Enzyme A does not recognize.
Starch's glucose units are joined by α bonds and cellulose's by β bonds; Enzyme A fits the α bond's shape.
Cellulose chains are much longer than starch chains, so Enzyme A ran out of time before it reached a bond it could cut.
Starch dissolves in water but cellulose does not, so Enzyme A could not reach the cellulose.

items.q: A student claims, "Glycogen is broken down faster than starch because glycogen is more branched." How well do these data support the claim?
options: Strongly, because glycogen released more sugar than starch did when Enzyme A was added to both.
Weakly: the gap is small and comes from one tube each, and branching was never tested.
Not at all, since glycogen and starch are built from different monomers and so are not comparable.
Strongly, because the no-enzyme tubes show that neither polysaccharide breaks down without help.

items.q: What is the main purpose of the no-enzyme tubes?
options: To show how much sugar each polysaccharide releases without enzyme, as a baseline for the enzyme tubes.
To show that the enzyme solutions themselves contain sugar that is released into the water over time.
To give the polysaccharides time to dissolve before the enzymes were added to the other tubes.
To check whether 37 °C is the best temperature for Enzymes A and B.

items.q: Termites eat wood but make little enzyme of their own like Enzyme B; microbes in their guts make it. Termites are given a treatment that kills their gut microbes and are then fed only wood. What is the most likely result?
options: The termites digest the wood as before, because wood also contains starch they can break down.
The termites starve, because most of the cellulose in the wood passes through them without being hydrolyzed.
The termites switch to making Enzyme A, which takes over the job of hydrolyzing the cellulose in the wood.
The termites build chitin from the wood instead, which they can digest with their own enzymes.

items.q: According to the model, what distinguishes α-glucose from β-glucose?
options: The direction of the –OH group on carbon 1: below the ring in α, above it in β.
The number of carbon atoms: α-glucose has six, and β-glucose has five.
The ring oxygen, which is present in α-glucose but replaced by carbon in β-glucose.
Their elements: β-glucose contains nitrogen, which is why cellulose is hard to digest.

items.q: Based on the model, why does cellulose form strong fibers while starch does not?
options: Cellulose chains are coiled more tightly than starch chains, which makes each one stronger.
Straight chains lie side by side, so –OH groups on neighboring chains form many hydrogen bonds.
Cellulose chains are joined to one another by covalent glycosidic bonds that run between neighboring chains.
Each cellulose monomer carries more –OH groups than a starch monomer, so cellulose dissolves faster.

items.q: Chitin's chains are built like the cellulose chains in the model, except each monomer has a nitrogen-containing group in place of one –OH. Which conclusion follows?
options: Chitin is a storage polysaccharide, because nitrogen makes its chains coil like starch.
Chitin can be digested by the same enzymes that hydrolyze starch, because both are made of sugars.
Building chitin uses some of the nitrogen an insect takes in; building cellulose uses none.
Chitin contains no glycosidic bonds, since its monomers carry nitrogen.

items.q: In the cellulose chain, two neighboring glucose units are joined through an oxygen between carbon 1 of one unit and carbon 4 of the next. How did this bond form?
options: By hydrolysis, which added a water molecule between the two glucose units.
By a hydrogen bond between the carbon-1 –OH of one glucose and the carbon-4 –OH of the next glucose.
By dehydration synthesis between two –OH groups, releasing water and leaving an oxygen bridge.
By an ionic bond between a positive carbon 1 and a negative carbon 4.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the data?
options: Glucose in the blood peaked highest after the glucose drink and stayed flat after the cellulose drink.
Starch raised glucose in the blood more than the glucose drink did, because starch is a larger molecule.
Sucrose raised glucose in the blood more than starch did at each time point.
Cellulose raised glucose in the blood slowly, peaking later than the other drinks.

items.q: The sucrose and glucose drinks each contained 50 g of sugar, but sucrose raised glucose in the blood much less. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Sucrose is not hydrolyzed by human enzymes, so most of it left the body undigested.
Hydrolyzing sucrose gives glucose and fructose, so about half of its sugar units are glucose.
Sucrose is a polysaccharide, so it takes much longer to break down than glucose.
Sucrose molecules are larger than glucose molecules, so 50 g of sucrose holds fewer carbon atoms.

items.q: Sucrose (C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>, mass 342) is hydrolyzed into glucose (mass 180) and fructose (mass 180). How many grams of glucose are released when the 50 g of sucrose is completely hydrolyzed? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Starch is a polymer of α-glucose, yet its curve rose more slowly than the glucose drink's. Which explanation fits the data and the structure of starch?
options: Starch must be hydrolyzed into glucose in the gut before the glucose can be absorbed.
Starch is made of β-glucose, which the body converts into α-glucose before absorbing it.
Starch contains fewer glucose units per gram than the glucose drink, because some of its mass is nitrogen.
Starch is absorbed whole into the blood and is broken down there more slowly.

items.q: A student hydrolyzes one molecule of maltose and one molecule of sucrose completely. Which monosaccharides does she get?
options: Two glucose and two fructose
Three glucose and one fructose
Two glucose, one fructose and one galactose
Four glucose

items.q: Which polysaccharide would you expect to find stored in a potato, and which in a human liver?
options: Starch in the potato; glycogen in the liver
Glycogen in the potato; starch in the liver
Cellulose in the potato; chitin in the liver
Starch in both, since both store α-glucose chains

items.q: A person who makes very little lactase (the enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose) drinks a glass of milk. Compared with a person who makes normal lactase, predict each value.

variables.name: Amount of lactose reaching the large intestine
Glucose absorbed into the blood from the milk
Number of glucose units in each lactose molecule

items.q: A newly discovered polysaccharide forms straight, unbranched chains that bind side by side through many hydrogen bonds and is not hydrolyzed by enzymes that digest starch. What is its most likely role in the organism?
options: Quick-release energy storage, like glycogen in animal muscles
Structural support, like cellulose in plant cell walls
Storing the instructions in genes, like DNA
Dissolved fuel carried in the blood, like glucose

items.q: Which molecule is a monosaccharide?
options: Fructose
Sucrose
Glycogen
Lactose

items.q: What do the four saturated fatty acids show about chain length and melting point?
options: Melting point rises as the chain gets longer.
Melting point falls as the chain gets longer.
Chain length has no clear effect, since the four are solid at room temperature.
Melting point rises with chain length, but the 18-carbon acid alone is solid at room temperature.

items.q: Stearic and oleic acids both have 18 carbons, but oleic acid melts 57 °C lower. Which explanation is best?
options: Oleic acid has two fewer hydrogen atoms, which makes each molecule lighter and easier to melt.
A cis double bond bends oleic acid's chain, so the chains cannot pack closely and attract each other less.
The double bond in oleic acid makes the chain polar, so it forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules instead.
Oleic acid's double bond is weaker than a single bond, so it breaks when the fatty acid melts.

items.q: A student claims that chain shape, not the number of hydrogen atoms, is what lowers the melting point of unsaturated fatty acids. Which comparison in the table gives the strongest evidence for this claim?
options: Stearic acid (70 °C) compared with lauric acid (44 °C)
Oleic acid (13 °C) compared with α-linolenic acid (−11 °C)
Oleic acid (13 °C) compared with elaidic acid (45 °C)
Stearic acid (70 °C) compared with oleic acid (13 °C)

items.q: Which of these fatty acids would be liquid at a room temperature of 22 °C? Select all that apply.
options: Lauric acid
Palmitic acid
Oleic acid
Elaidic acid
Stearic acid

items.q: Across the saturated fatty acids from lauric (12 carbons) to stearic (18 carbons), by how many °C does the melting point rise, on average, for each 2 carbons added to the chain? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which statement best describes the data?
options: The colder the water, the higher the percent of unsaturated tails in the fish's membrane phospholipids.
The warmer the water, the higher the percent of unsaturated tails in the fish's membrane phospholipids.
The percent of unsaturated tails stayed about the same between 5 °C and 30 °C.
The percent of unsaturated tails fell sharply between 5 °C and 10 °C and stayed level above that.

items.q: Using the values at 5 °C and 30 °C, by how many percentage points does the unsaturated share fall for each 1 °C rise in water temperature? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the higher percent of unsaturated tails in fish kept in cold water?
options: Unsaturated tails release more energy when broken down, which helps the fish produce heat in cold water.
Kinked unsaturated tails pack loosely, so the membrane stays flexible instead of stiffening as the water cools.
Cold water contains less dissolved fat, so the fish take up mostly unsaturated fatty acids from their food.
Unsaturated tails are more hydrophilic, so they help the membrane mix with the colder water around it.

items.q: Fish from the 25 °C tank are moved to a 5 °C tank and kept there for four weeks. Predict how each value for their membrane phospholipids changes over those weeks.

variables.name: Percent of tails that are unsaturated
Temperature at which the membrane lipids would become stiff and gel-like
Number of fatty acid tails on each phospholipid

items.q: Which feature of the study best supports the conclusion that water temperature caused the change in membrane fatty acids, rather than just being correlated with it?
options: The researchers set each tank's temperature and kept food and light the same for every group.
The points fall on a nearly straight line, which shows that the temperature caused the change.
The fish came from one supplier, so each fish started with identical membranes.
Ten fish were measured in each group, so the averages are not affected by chance.

items.q: Phospholipids are shaken into a beaker of water. Which arrangement are they most likely to form?
options: A double layer with tails facing each other in the middle and heads facing the water on both sides
A double layer with heads facing each other in the middle and tails facing the water on both sides
A single layer lying flat on the bottom of the beaker, with heads and tails pointing in random directions
Separate molecules spread evenly through the water, like dissolved salt

items.q: How many water molecules are released when a cell builds 4 triglyceride molecules from glycerol and fatty acids?

A small bird needs 740 kJ of energy for a long nonstop flight. Fat yields 37 kJ per gram and glycogen 17 kJ per gram. How many more grams of fuel would it need to carry if it stored the energy as glycogen instead of fat? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which feature of fatty acids best explains why fats store more energy per gram than carbohydrates?
options: Fatty acid chains are mostly C–H and C–C bonds and carry far less oxygen per carbon than sugars do.
Fats are polymers with many more monomers per molecule than carbohydrates, so each molecule holds more bonds.
Fatty acids contain phosphorus, which stores extra energy in the bonds around it.
Fats are hydrophobic, so they hold their energy in the water they exclude.

items.q: Why do phospholipids form bilayers in water while triglycerides form oily droplets instead?
options: Triglycerides are heavier than phospholipids, so they sink to the bottom and pool together in droplets.
Phospholipids have a polar head to face the water; triglycerides have none, so they cluster away from water.
Triglycerides have three tails, which are too many to fit in the middle of a bilayer.
Phospholipids are saturated and triglycerides are unsaturated, so phospholipids alone pack into flat sheets.

items.q: Which feature identifies a lipid as a steroid?
options: A skeleton of four fused carbon rings
A glycerol bonded to three fatty acids
A phosphate-containing head and two fatty acid tails
A long chain with no carbon-carbon double bonds

items.q: Estrogen, a steroid hormone, passes straight through the lipid bilayer of a cell membrane, but a hormone made of a chain of amino acids does not. Which explanation is best?
options: Estrogen is a smaller molecule than any protein, and the bilayer lets small molecules through whatever their chemistry.
Estrogen is hydrophobic, so it dissolves into the nonpolar middle of the bilayer; a polar protein hormone does not.
Estrogen carries a phosphate head like a phospholipid, so the bilayer takes it in as one of its own.
Protein hormones are broken down by hydrolysis as soon as they touch the bilayer.

items.q: Which of these molecules are lipids? Select all that apply.
options: Cholesterol
Glycogen
A triglyceride from olive oil
Cellulose
A phospholipid
An amino acid

items.q: Which pattern holds for the DNA of the four organisms (human, wheat, yeast and E. coli)?
options: The four bases are present in about equal amounts in each organism.
%A is close to %T, and %G is close to %C, though the values differ between organisms.
%A is close to %G, and %T is close to %C, in each organism.
Each organism has the same base percentages, since their DNA is built from the same four nucleotides.

items.q: Which conclusion about Virus X is best supported by the data?
options: Its DNA is single-stranded, since its %A does not match its %T and its %G does not match its %C.
Its DNA contains uracil in place of thymine, since its values do not follow the pattern of the organisms.
Its DNA is double-stranded but contains more hydrogen bonds than the organisms' DNA.
Its measurements are less reliable than the others, since a virus is too small to give accurate data.

items.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA from a new species is 21% guanine. What percent of its bases are adenine? Give a whole number.
Why does the DNA of each organism contain nearly equal amounts of adenine and thymine?
options: Cells make adenine and thymine at exactly the same rate, so they enter DNA in equal numbers.
Each A on one strand pairs with a T on the other, so across both strands the counts match.
Adenine and thymine are bonded to each other within one strand by the sugar-phosphate backbone.
Adenine and thymine are isomers, so the cell produces them together whenever it builds new DNA.

items.q: The researchers next analyze a virus whose genes are carried in single-stranded RNA. Which result is most likely?
options: Uracil in place of thymine, with %A and %U that need not match.
Thymine and uracil both present, with %T equal to %U.
Uracil in place of thymine, with %A exactly equal to %U because they pair.
The same four bases as DNA, with %G equal to %C.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship shown in the graph?
options: As G + C content rises, the temperature needed to separate half the DNA rises steadily.
As G + C content increases, the temperature needed to separate half the DNA decreases.
The temperature rises with G + C content up to 52% and then levels off.
G + C content has little effect, since the six temperatures differ by less than a few degrees.

items.q: Using the first and last points, by how many °C does the separation temperature rise for each 1% increase in G + C content? Give your answer to two decimal places.
Which explanation for the trend would the exam expect?
options: G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs two, so G–C-rich DNA needs more heat to separate.
G–C pairs are joined by covalent bonds, which are stronger than the hydrogen bonds joining A–T pairs.
G and C are heavier bases, so the strands rich in them move apart more slowly when the DNA is heated.
Heating breaks the sugar-phosphate backbone, and G–C-rich backbones are stronger.

items.q: DNA from a seventh species has a G + C content of 50%. At about what temperature would half of it separate under the same conditions?
options: About 84 °C
About 90 °C
About 95 °C
About 100 °C

items.q: A student concludes, "Bacteria that live in hot springs must have DNA with a high G + C content." How well do these data support that conclusion?
options: Strongly, because the data show that a higher G + C content raises the temperature that DNA can withstand.
Weakly: they show a test-tube effect of G + C content but say nothing about where any species lives.
Hardly, because the G + C content of DNA makes little difference to how it responds to heat.
Strongly, because the six species include some with G + C contents above 60%.

items.q: What is the sequence of Strand 2, written from its 5′ end to its 3′ end?
options: 5′-TACCGTAAG-3′
5′-GAATGCCAT-3′
5′-ATGGCATTC-3′

options: The left end, labeled 5′
The right end, labeled 3′
Both ends, since each nucleotide has a phosphate
Neither end, since the phosphates link to the bases

items.q: An RNA molecule has the same base sequence as Strand 1, except that RNA uses its own bases. What is the RNA's sequence?
options: 5′-AUGGCAUUC-3′
5′-ATGGCATTC-3′

items.q: Which three parts make up a single nucleotide?
options: A phosphate, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base
An amino group, a carboxyl group and a side group
Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group
A six-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base

items.q: Which features does RNA have that DNA does not? Select all that apply.
options: Ribose sugar
Phosphate groups in its backbone
The base uracil
A 5′ end and a 3′ end
The base guanine

items.q: When DNA is heated to 95 °C, its two strands separate, but each strand stays one long chain. Which explanation is best?
options: Hydrogen bonds join the bases across the strands and heat breaks them; covalent bonds hold each backbone and stay intact.
Heat breaks the covalent bonds between bases, but the hydrogen bonds in each backbone are strong enough to survive the heat.
Heat breaks the backbone into separate nucleotides, which stay joined to their partners by their bases.
The two strands repel each other at high temperature because both carry negative phosphate groups.

items.q: Two DNA molecules from different genes are each exactly 1,000 base pairs long and each 25% A, 25% T, 25% G and 25% C. Which statement about them is most accurate?
options: They carry the same information, since their base percentages are identical.
They can carry different information, since their base order can differ.
They have identical sequences, since DNA pairs A with T and G with C in each molecule.
They are unlikely to both be real genes, since genes differ in base percentages.

items.q: Which statement best describes the pattern in the data?
options: Swaps that kept similar chemistry had little effect; a charge buried in the core had the largest.
Each of the six changes reduced the enzyme's activity by about the same amount, whatever the side chain.
Changes at the surface reduced activity more than changes in the core.
Swapping a positive side chain for a negative one had the largest effect of the six.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the very low activity of V2?
options: A buried charged side chain disrupts the hydrophobic core, so the chain folds into a different shape.
Aspartic acid breaks peptide bonds near position 45, cutting Enzyme Q into two pieces.
Aspartic acid is a larger amino acid than leucine, so it makes the whole polypeptide too long to fold.
The new side chain forms a disulfide bridge with cysteine 78, locking the core in the wrong place.

items.q: Serine differs from cysteine only in having –OH where cysteine has –SH. Why did V5 lose most of its activity?
options: Serine's –OH group makes the core so polar that the whole protein falls apart into its separate amino acids.
Without an –SH at position 78, the disulfide bridge to cysteine 150 cannot form, so that fold is no longer locked.
Serine does not form peptide bonds, so the chain is broken at position 78.
Serine's –OH group forms a new disulfide bridge with cysteine 150 that holds that part of the protein too tightly.

items.q: Researchers plan a seventh version with a different amino acid at position 45. Which replacement for leucine is most likely to leave activity close to normal?
options: Lysine, which has a positively charged side chain
Glutamic acid, which has a negatively charged side chain
Valine, which has a nonpolar side chain
Serine, which has a polar side chain with an –OH group

items.q: A student claims that where a change happens in a protein matters more than how different the new side chain is. Which pair of versions gives the best evidence for this claim?
options: V1 and V2, which both change the buried position 45
V3 and V4, which both change the surface position 112
V2 and V4: a new negative charge at two positions
V5 and V6, which end with similar activities

items.q: What does Sample B show?
options: Breaking the bonds that hold its shape removes nearly all of the enzyme's activity.
Urea and the reducing agent break the enzyme into its separate amino acids.
The enzyme's activity is not affected by the loss of its shape.
The enzyme keeps about half of its activity when its disulfide bridges are broken by the agent.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the result for Sample C?
options: The sequence alone holds the information needed to refold into the working shape.
Urea is needed for the enzyme to fold correctly in cells, so removing it slowly helped.
The enzyme needs chaperone proteins to fold into its working shape inside the tube.
Disulfide bridges do not affect the enzyme's shape or activity.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the 1% activity of Sample D?
options: The reducing agent destroyed some of the enzyme's peptide bonds before it could be removed by dialysis.
In urea, cysteines paired at random as bridges re-formed, locking most chains into wrong shapes.
The urea had permanently changed the sequence of amino acids in the chain.
The enzyme in D had too few cysteines left to make any disulfide bridges.

items.q: If the 8 cysteines paired up at random into 4 disulfide bridges, how many different sets of pairings are possible? (Hint: the first cysteine can pair with any of the other 7; the next unpaired cysteine with any of the remaining 5; and so on.)
In Sample B, which level of the enzyme's structure is left intact?
options: Primary structure, because urea and the reducing agent do not break peptide bonds
Secondary structure, because α helices are held by covalent bonds
Tertiary structure, because hydrophobic interactions are too strong for urea to break apart
Quaternary structure, because the enzyme has several subunits

items.q: What makes one amino acid different from another?
options: Its R group (side chain)
Its number of amino groups
The type of bond it forms with the next amino acid
Whether it contains carbon

items.q: Two amino acids are joined by a peptide bond. Between which atoms does the new bond form?
options: Between the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid and the amino nitrogen of the next
Between the R groups of the two amino acids
Between the two central carbons, which share a pair of electrons directly with each other
Between the nitrogen atoms of the two amino groups

items.q: What holds an α helix in its coiled shape?
options: Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups a few positions apart
Disulfide bridges between neighboring cysteines that lie in the same chain
Peptide bonds that link each amino acid to the fourth one along the chain
Hydrophobic interactions between side chains inside the coil

items.q: Which of these would change a protein's primary structure? Select all that apply.
options: Replacing one amino acid with a different one
Heating the protein until it unfolds
Moving it to a solution with a very different pH
Breaking one of its disulfide bridges
Adding a chaperone protein

items.q: In the inherited disorder that makes red blood cells sickle-shaped, valine (nonpolar) replaces glutamic acid (charged) at a position on the outer surface of a hemoglobin subunit. Which explanation best accounts for the problem this causes?
options: A nonpolar patch on the surface sticks to nonpolar areas of other hemoglobin molecules, forming long fibers.
Valine breaks the peptide bonds around it, so the hemoglobin chain falls apart into several shorter pieces.
The change removes a disulfide bridge, so the four subunits come apart.
Valine carries a positive charge that repels the other subunits of the same hemoglobin molecule.

items.q: An egg white protein is heated until it turns from clear to white. Predict how each feature of the protein changes.

variables.name: Number of peptide bonds in each chain
Number of hydrogen bonds holding helices and sheets
Number of nonpolar side chains exposed to water

items.q: Cells make many chaperone proteins when they are heated. What is the most likely reason?
options: Heat partly unfolds proteins, and chaperones help them refold correctly instead of clumping together.
Chaperones break heated proteins down into amino acids so that new proteins can be built.
Chaperones change the amino acid sequences of heated proteins to make them stable at high temperature.
Chaperones replace heat-damaged proteins and do their jobs for them.

items.q: Put these steps in order as a newly made hemoglobin chain becomes part of a working hemoglobin molecule.
options: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds in the sequence set by the gene.
Backbone hydrogen bonds coil parts of the chain into α helices.
Nonpolar side chains cluster inside as the chain folds into its 3-D shape.
Four folded chains assemble into one hemoglobin molecule.

items.q: A protein dissolves in the watery fluid of blood. Where would most of its leucine and valine side chains (both nonpolar) most likely be found?
options: On the outer surface, where they make the protein dissolve in the fluid
Buried in the protein's interior, away from water
Spread evenly between the surface and the interior of the protein
Joined to each other by disulfide bridges on the surface
